title: The Lesson I Learned From Archippus
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Archippus
The Forgotten Man in Scripture Who Exposed My Excuses, Confronted My Comfort, and Reminded Me That Jesus Finishes What He Starts
Most Christians know Peter.
Many know Paul.
Some know Timothy.
But almost nobody talks about Archippus.
And maybe that's exactly why his story matters.
Because most of us are not standing on a stage.
Most of us are not writing books of the Bible.
Most of us are not leading nations, churches, or movements.
Most of us are simply trying to remain faithful in the ordinary places where God has planted us.
And that is where Archippus quietly steps out of the shadows of Scripture and looks directly into our hearts.
His name appears only briefly, yet the lesson he leaves behind has the power to change an entire life.
In Colossians 4:17, Paul writes:
The original Greek reads:
"Καὶ εἴπατε Ἀρχίππῳ· Βλέπε τὴν διακονίαν ἣν παρέλαβες ἐν Κυρίῳ, ἵνα αὐτὴν πληροῖς."
Transliterated:
"Kai eipate Archippō; Blepe tēn diakonian hēn parelabes en Kyriō, hina autēn plērois."
A faithful rendering would be:
"Tell Archippus: Pay careful attention to the ministry you received in the Lord, so that you may complete it."
Not start it.
Complete it.
That single word pierced me.
Complete it.
Because starting is exciting.
Finishing is costly.
Starting gets applause.
Finishing requires endurance.
Starting feels spiritual.
Finishing demands surrender.
The longer I walked with Christ, the more I realized that many believers struggle not because they never receive a calling from God, but because they become distracted before fulfilling it.
Life happens.
Disappointments happen.
Church hurt happens.
Financial pressure happens.
Fatigue happens.
Fear happens.
And slowly the fire that once burned brightly becomes a small hidden ember beneath layers of excuses.
Archippus reminds us that God notices unfinished assignments.
Not because He is cruel.
Not because He is demanding perfection.
But because He loves us too much to watch us abandon the purpose He entrusted to us.
The remarkable thing is that Paul did not tell Archippus to find a new ministry.
He did not tell him to reinvent himself.
He did not tell him to chase a bigger platform.
He simply told him to pay attention to what he had already received from the Lord.
That is a word many of us desperately need.
We live in a culture obsessed with the next thing.
The next opportunity.
The next breakthrough.
The next promotion.
The next ministry.
The next audience.
The next season.
Meanwhile God keeps asking:
"What did you do with what I already gave you?"
That question is uncomfortable.
Because it exposes something we rarely want to admit.
Sometimes we are waiting for a new assignment while neglecting the current one.
And if we are honest, some of us know exactly what God has been asking us to do.
The conversation we have avoided.
The ministry we have neglected.
The person we need to forgive.
The prayer life we once had.
The Bible reading we abandoned.
The faith we slowly allowed to become casual.
Archippus stands as a living reminder that God's callings are not accidents.
The ministry Paul referenced was something Archippus had "received in the Lord."
The Greek word "παρέλαβες" (parelabes) means to receive, accept, or take hold of something entrusted to you.
It was not self-created.
It was entrusted.
And that changes everything.
Because what God entrusts carries responsibility.
Yet here is where the Gospel becomes breathtakingly beautiful.
The story is not ultimately about Archippus.
It is about Jesus.
Because every unfinished story in Scripture points us toward the One who finishes perfectly.
Where Adam failed, Christ succeeded.
Where Israel stumbled, Christ obeyed.
Where we quit, Christ remained faithful.
On the cross, Jesus cried out:
"Τετέλεσται" (Tetelestai).
"It is finished."
John 19:30.
Not partially completed.
Not almost accomplished.
Finished.
Paid in full.
Perfectly fulfilled.
Every prophecy.
Every requirement.
Every promise.
Every step of redemption.
Completed by the Son of God.
That is why the lesson of Archippus is not a message of guilt.
It is a message of grace.
Because the same Christ who completed His mission is still empowering His people to complete theirs.
Some readers may feel disqualified right now.
You remember who you used to be.
You remember your failures.
You remember the scandal.
The addiction.
The secret sin.
The broken marriage.
The wasted years.
The rebellion.
The shame.
The regret.
But the Gospel has always been a story of God rewriting ruined lives.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed adultery.
Paul persecuted believers.
Mary Magdalene carried a painful past.
Yet Jesus transformed every one of their stories.
That is why our message remains unchanged:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why Archippus resonates so deeply with me.
His story feels unfinished.
We do not know how he responded.
We do not know whether he struggled.
We do not know whether he felt discouraged.
We do not know whether he felt inadequate.
We only know he was told to complete what God had given him.
And perhaps Scripture leaves the ending open because now the question becomes ours.
Will we complete what God has entrusted to us?
Will we remain faithful when nobody is watching?
Will we obey when obedience costs something?
Will we continue when we are tired?
Will we trust Christ when the road becomes difficult?
That question lingers long after we finish reading.
Because every believer is writing a testimony.
Every believer is living a chapter.
Every believer is carrying an assignment from God.
And one day we will stand before Jesus.
Not to earn salvation.
That was secured by His grace alone.
But to give an account for what we did with what He entrusted to us.
Maybe today is the day you stop running.
Maybe today is the day you pick up what you laid down.
Maybe today is the day you return to the calling, the ministry, the prayer life, the obedience, and the faithfulness that Christ placed before you.
If this message spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
Because someone else's journey from scandal to grace may begin with the article you chose to share today.
One forgotten name in Scripture became a reminder that God has not forgotten yours.
